name: Pontine horizontal gaze palsy
presentation: After a pontine stroke the patient cannot look toward the side of the lesion with either eye, and at rest the eyes drift toward the opposite side, away from the lesion and toward any hemiparesis. This is the reverse of the hemispheric pattern, where the eyes look toward the lesion and away from the weak limbs. Distinguishing the two is a bedside way to tell a pontine from a hemispheric stroke.

deficits.sign: Gaze palsy toward the lesion; eyes deviated away from the lesion
Hemiparesis when the basis pontis is involved; the eyes look toward the weak side
Oculocephalic reflex overcomes a PPRF lesion but not an abducens nuclear lesion

reasoning: The frontal eye field of each hemisphere sends its saccade command across the midline to the paramedian pontine reticular formation of the opposite side, which fires the adjacent abducens nucleus to move both eyes toward that side. A right hemispheric lesion therefore removes the drive to the left PPRF: the patient cannot look left, and the unopposed left hemisphere pushes the eyes to the right, toward the lesion; with the crossed corticospinal fibers also damaged, the weak limbs are on the left, so the eyes look away from the hemiparesis. A left pontine lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus removes leftward gaze at its final stage: the eyes cannot look left, toward the lesion, and drift right, away from it; the uncrossed corticospinal fibers in the left basis pontis produce a right hemiparesis, so now the eyes look toward the weak limbs. The vestibulo-ocular reflex reaches the abducens nucleus directly from the vestibular nuclei, bypassing the PPRF, so a PPRF lesion (supranuclear) can be overcome by head turning and caloric stimulation whereas an abducens nuclear lesion cannot, and a nuclear lesion adds an ipsilateral facial palsy from the facial colliculus.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the dorsal paramedian caudal pons; may extend ventrally into the corticospinal fibers.

mimics.name: Frontal eye field lesion
mimics.howToDistinguish: Eyes deviate toward the lesion, palsy overcome by the oculocephalic reflex, resolves within days

mimics.name: Sixth nerve palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Only one eye fails to abduct; the other adducts normally

mimics.name: Seizure with gaze deviation
mimics.howToDistinguish: Eyes deviate away from an irritative focus and jerk; transient

management: Bedside: use the direction of gaze deviation relative to the weak side to localize before imaging
Recovery of gaze is usual over weeks
